a: For the music director. A psalm of David.
p: Hebrew Bibles count a psalm's title as verse 1, so most verses in this part are one number higher there.
b: This site follows the English numbering, where the title is verse 0 and the psalm proper starts at verse 1. Hebrew Bibles (and many Jewish and scholarly works) count the title as verse 1 when it is more than a few words long. So Psalm 31:5 here is Psalm 31:6 in a Hebrew Bible, and Psalm 40:6 is Hebrew 40:7. Where the title is only two words ("Of David", Psalms 32, 35, 37), the Hebrew joins it to the first line and the numbers stay the same. The Greek and Latin also number the psalms themselves one lower in this stretch: Psalms 31–41 are Psalms 30–40 in the Septuagint, the Vulgate and older Catholic and Orthodox books. Witnesses for this part: the Old Greek was checked in Rahlfs' edition (as printed online at blueletterbible.org), and the contents of the Qumran scrolls 4QPs-a, 4QPs-c and 4QPs-q in an English edition (dssenglishbible.com). Other readings (Hebrew manuscripts, the Syriac, the Targum, the Qumran commentary 4Q171) are given as reported by the editions and commentaries cited.

a: I take shelter in you, LORD
p: Chasah means to run for cover, as a bird or a traveler does. It runs through Book I like a refrain.
b: The verb chasah pictures someone running under cover from a storm or an attack (Isaiah 30:2; Judges 9:15). In the psalms it becomes the word for trusting God when you are in danger. It frames Psalm 31 (31:1, 31:19) and closes Psalm 34 (34:8, 34:22) and Psalm 37 (37:40). Older English Bibles say "trust"; the Hebrew picture is more physical: God is the shelter you run into.

a: Rescue me, because you are righteous
p: "In your righteousness" does not mean the psalmist's goodness but God's faithfulness to put things right.
b: Literally "in your righteousness rescue me". In the psalms God's tsedaqah is his loyal, saving justice: he keeps his word and sets things right for those who are wronged. So the poet can ask to be rescued because God is righteous. Luther's first lectures on the Psalms (1513–15) wrestled with "in your righteousness" (31:1; 71:2), the question that led him to his reading of Romans 1:17: God's righteousness is the gift by which he saves, not only the standard by which he judges.

a: Become a strong rock for me
p: Verses 1–3 echo the opening of Psalm 71 almost word for word, and David's song in 2 Samuel 22.
b: Verses 1–3 reappear with small changes as Psalm 71:1–3, and the pile-up of names for God (rock, fortress, stronghold) recalls David's song of thanks (2 Samuel 22:2–3; Psalm 18:2). In the hill country of Judah a high rock was the safest place in a raid; David hid among such crags in the wilderness (1 Samuel 23:25–28). Calling God a rock says he cannot be moved and cannot be stormed.

a: Into your hand I place my spirit.
p: Luke's Jesus dies praying this line, Stephen echoes it, and Jews and Christians still say it at bedtime.
b: In Luke, Jesus' last words on the cross are this verse, with "Father" added: "Father, into your hands I entrust my spirit" (Luke 23:46, a fresh rendering). Stephen, dying, prays "Lord Jesus, receive my spirit" (Acts 7:59), and Peter tells suffering believers to "entrust their souls to a faithful Creator" (1 Peter 4:19). In the psalm the line is the prayer of someone in danger handing his life over to God for safekeeping, not yet a prayer for the moment of death. The Jewish bedtime prayers use it, and the last stanza of the hymn Adon Olam takes it up: "into his hand I place my spirit" as I sleep and wake. In the Western church it is the responsory of night prayer (Compline), In manus tuas, Domine.

a: faithful God
p: 'El 'emet is literally "God of faithfulness" or "God of truth". 'Emet is what holds firm.
b: 'Emet comes from the root of "amen": what is firm, reliable, true. "God of truth" (KJV) is not wrong, but the sense here is that God can be relied on: he does what he says. The poet has just put his life in God's hand, so the next thing he says is that the hand is trustworthy.

a: empty nothings
p: Havlei shav, "breaths of emptiness", is a scornful name for idols, as in Jonah 2:8.
b: Hevel is a breath or puff of air (the word of Ecclesiastes, and of 39:5 here); shav' is emptiness or falsehood. Together they mean things with nothing in them, and the phrase is used for idols (Jeremiah 8:19; Jonah 2:8, the only other place with the same phrase). "Those who devote themselves to" is literally "those who keep" or "guard" them, a verb used for keeping God's laws. Some Hebrew manuscripts, the Greek and the Syriac read "you hate" for "I hate"; the Plain follows the Masoretic Text.

a: a wide-open place
p: Distress in Hebrew is a tight place; rescue is a broad place. The same picture closes many laments.
b: The word for trouble, tsarah, comes from a root meaning narrow or tight. Rescue is merchav, a wide space. The psalmist has been hemmed in by a net (31:4); now he can walk freely. The picture returns in 18:19 and 118:5.

a: Through my guilt my strength has stumbled
p: The Hebrew says "by my guilt"; the Greek and Syriac say "in my poverty", one letter different.
b: The Masoretic Text has ba'avoni, "by my iniquity". The Greek translator read be'oni, "in my affliction" or "poverty" (Greek en ptōcheia), and the Syriac agrees. The two words differ by one letter in Hebrew. Nothing else in the psalm speaks of the poet's sin, so many scholars think "misery" is the older reading (the NRSV follows it). Others note that sickness and guilt are often joined in laments (38:3; 41:4). See the variant.

a: to my neighbors, very much so
p: Me'od, "very", stands oddly here. Scholars propose small changes, but no witness has a different text.
b: The Hebrew is literally "to my neighbors, very". The word me'od ("very, much") normally qualifies a verb or adjective, so many scholars suspect a copying slip. One proposal is manod, "a head-shaking" (a gesture of scorn, compare 44:14). The Greek has "exceedingly", like the Hebrew. The Plain keeps the Hebrew as it stands: to the neighbors, "very much so".

a: like a smashed pot
p: A cracked clay pot was thrown out; its shards lay everywhere in an ancient town. Nobody missed it.
b: Pottery was cheap and broke easily, and broken pieces (potsherds) were thrown on the rubbish heap or used for scraping (Job 2:8). To be like a broken pot is to be useless and forgotten, like the dead the poet has just named. Jeremiah uses the image for King Jehoiachin (Jeremiah 22:28), and smashes a jar as a sign of Jerusalem's ruin (Jeremiah 19:10–11).

a: "Terror all around!"
p: Magor missaviv, "terror all around", is Jeremiah's favorite phrase, and he too hears it whispered.
b: The phrase magor missaviv appears five times in Jeremiah (Jeremiah 6:25; Jeremiah 20:3, as a name; Jeremiah 20:10; Jeremiah 46:5; Jeremiah 49:29), and in a varied form in Lamentations 2:22. Jeremiah 20:10 matches this verse closely: he too hears "the whispering of many" and then the cry. Either the prophet knew the psalm, the psalm borrowed from the prophet, or both used a common saying. Many scholars see Jeremiah's language all through Psalm 31.

a: My times are in your hand.
p: "Times" are the turns of a life: its seasons, its dangers and its end. All of them sit in God's hand.
b: 'Ittotai, "my times", is plural: the moments and events of a life, good and bad (compare 1 Chronicles 29:30, "the times that swept over him"). The poet has just put his spirit in God's hand (31:5); now he says his whole life story is there. The next line plays on the word: get me out of the hand of my enemies. Two hands are reaching for him, and he prefers God's.

a: Shine your face on your servant
p: The line takes up the blessing of Aaron: "may the LORD make his face shine toward you".
b: The priestly blessing of Aaron includes the line "May the LORD make his face shine toward you and be gracious to you" (Numbers 6:25). Psalms turn that blessing into a prayer (4:6; 67:1; 80:3, 7, 19). A shining face is a friendly, favorable face, the opposite of God hiding his face (30:7).

a: in a city ringed by siege
p: Literally "in a city of siege": a real siege, a picture, or (by emendation) "a time of distress".
b: Be'ir matsor is "in a city of siege" or "a fortified city" (KJV "a strong city"; the Greek "in a city of encirclement"). Readers who take the title as history link it to David at Keilah, where Saul tried to trap him inside a walled town (1 Samuel 23:7–13). Others read it as an image: God's love surrounded him like walls. Some scholars change one letter and read be'et matsor, "in a time of distress". No manuscript has that reading.

a: in my panic
p: Bechofzi means "in my alarm" or "when I ran in fright". The KJV's "in my haste" sounds like a hasty remark.
b: Chafaz is to rush off in fear (2 Samuel 4:4, the nurse who fled with Mephibosheth; 1 Samuel 23:26, David hurrying to escape Saul). "I said in my haste" (KJV) can sound as if the poet spoke too quickly. The point is that he spoke out of terror. The Greek has "in my ecstasy" (ekstasei), and the Greek title of the psalm adds "of ecstasy" from this verse. Jonah 2:4 uses a similar line: "I have been driven away from before your eyes".

a: every one of his faithful
p: Chasidim are people marked by hesed, loyal love. The word later named Jewish movements of piety.
b: Chasidav, "his faithful ones" (KJV "saints"), comes from hesed, the loyal love that the psalm praises (31:7, 16, 21). They are people who return God's loyalty with their own. The same word later named the Hasideans of the Maccabean age (1 Maccabees 2:42) and the Hasidic movement of the 1700s.

a: A maskil.
p: Psalm 32 is the first of thirteen psalms called maskil. The meaning is uncertain: a skillful song, or a teaching song.
b: Maskil comes from sakal, "to be wise, to give insight, to succeed". Thirteen psalm titles use it (32, 42, 44, 45, 52–55, 74, 78, 88, 89, 142). Proposed meanings: a "teaching psalm" (the verb returns in 32:8, "I will make you wise"); an "artful" or skillful song; or a song that gives success. The Greek translates synesis, "understanding"; the Latin intellectus. Psalm 47:7 uses the word as an instruction to sing "skillfully". The site keeps the word as it is, as most modern versions do.

a: Happy is the one whose rebellion is lifted away
p: Paul quotes 32:1–2 in Romans 4 as David's witness that God counts people right apart from works.
b: In Romans 4:6–8 Paul quotes these two verses from the Greek: "Happy are those whose lawless deeds are forgiven and whose sins are covered; happy is the man whose sin the Lord will not count" (a fresh rendering). He uses them beside Genesis 15:6: God "counts" righteousness to Abraham, and does not "count" sin to David. Jewish readers hear the verses as the joy of repentance and forgiveness under the covenant, and note that the psalm goes on to require confession (32:5). Christian traditions differ on what Paul draws from it (see the chapter page).

a: rebellion
p: Pesha' (rebellion), chata'ah (missing the mark) and 'avon (twisted guilt) appear together, as in Exodus 34:7.
b: The psalm uses all three main Hebrew words for wrongdoing. Pesha' is rebellion, breaking faith with a ruler or a partner. Chata'ah is sin, failing or missing the mark. 'Avon is crookedness, and also the guilt and penalty it brings. The three forgiving verbs match: the sin is "lifted away" (nasa', carried off), "covered" (kasah), and "not counted". The same three nouns stand in God's self-description to Moses (Exodus 34:7) and in Psalm 51:1–3.

a: covered over
p: Kasah, "cover", is not kipper, "atone". The point is that God hides sin from view.
b: The verb is kasah, to cover or conceal, not the priestly word kipper ("make atonement"), though both have been linked to the idea of covering. The play is deliberate: when the poet covers his own sin it destroys him (32:3–4), but when he stops covering it (32:5, the same verb) God covers it. Proverbs 28:13 says the same thing.

a: whose spirit holds no trickery
p: Remiyyah is deceit. The forgiven person is the one who has stopped hiding, not one who never sinned.
b: Remiyyah means deceit or slackness. In context it is the self-deceit of the person who will not admit his sin (32:3). Jesus' greeting of Nathanael, "a true Israelite in whom there is no deceit" (John 1:47, a fresh rendering), may echo this verse in the Greek, which uses dolos and reads "in his mouth" where the Hebrew has "in his spirit" (see the variant).

a: My sap was turned, as in the droughts of summer.
p: Leshaddi is a rare word, probably "my sap" or "my strength". The Greek read it quite differently.
b: The Hebrew has nehpakh leshaddi becharvonei qayits, roughly "my sap was turned, as by the droughts of summer". Leshad occurs again only in Numbers 11:8, of manna tasting like "cakes baked with oil" (something moist and rich). So most take it as the body's moisture or vigor. The Greek has "I was turned into misery when a thorn was stuck in me", reading different words from the same letters. See the variant.

a: I will confess my rebellious acts to the LORD
p: Confession is the turning point of the psalm. Traditions differ on whether it must ever be made to a priest.
b: The poem turns on this verse: silence wore him out (32:3–4); speaking brought release. Jewish tradition makes confession (viddui) a core part of repentance, especially on the Day of Atonement, and Maimonides begins his laws of repentance with spoken confession to God. Christians read the psalm as one of the seven penitential psalms. The churches differ on whether confession to God alone is enough or confession to a priest is also required for serious sin (see the chapter page).

a: at the time for finding you
p: Le'et metso, "at a time of finding", is short and odd. Some read "in a time of distress", others "only".
b: Literally "for a time of finding". Isaiah 55:6 says "seek the LORD while he may be found", and most readers take this verse the same way. Some scholars, noting how cramped the line is, propose small changes: le'et matsoq, "in a time of distress", or reading the next word raq ("surely, only") with the line before. The meaning stays close either way: pray now, before the flood comes.

a: when the great waters flood
p: Mayim rabbim, "many waters", is the Bible's name for the chaos of floods and death.
b: "Many" or "great waters" stand for overwhelming danger: the flood, the sea, death (18:16; 69:1–2; 144:7). God is the one who rules them (29:3; 93:4). The faithful person who prays will not be swept away, while the stubborn horse and mule of 32:9 must be dragged.

a: "I will make you wise and show you
p: God may speak here, or the forgiven poet now teaching others. The Hebrew does not say.
b: There is no "he said". Many readers hear God's voice answering the psalmist (compare "my eye on you" and 33:18). Others (Calvin, many modern scholars) hear the poet himself, who promised in 51:13 to teach sinners God's ways; having been forgiven, he now instructs others, which is what a maskil does (the verb here is askilkha, from the same root). The Plain marks verses 8–9 as a quotation without naming the speaker.

a: otherwise it will not come near you
p: The Hebrew may mean "else it will not come to you" or "so that it does not come near you".
b: Literally "with bit and bridle its ornament to curb, not coming near to you". 'Edyo, "its ornament", is odd; it may mean the horse's harness, or (by a different word) its "mouth" or "spirit". The last words can mean that without a bridle the animal will not come to you, or that the bridle keeps it from charging at you (so the KJV, "lest they come near"). Either way, the person who confesses freely is set against a beast that must be forced.
orig: עֶדְיוֹ לִבְלוֹם בַּל קְרֹב אֵלֶיךָ ('edyo livlom bal qerov eleikha)

a: Shout for joy, you righteous, in the LORD!
p: Psalm 33 is the only psalm in Book I after Psalm 2 with no title in Hebrew. Some think it once belonged with Psalm 32.
b: Every psalm in Psalms 3–41 has a title except 10 and 33. Psalm 10 probably once ran on from Psalm 9 (the two share one acrostic). Psalm 33 begins where Psalm 32 ends: 32:11 calls the righteous to "shout for joy", and 33:1 repeats the call. Some Hebrew manuscripts join the two. The Greek gives it the title "Of David". Two Qumran scrolls (4QPs-a and 4QPs-q) seem to have no Psalm 32 at all: in 4QPs-q, Psalm 33 follows Psalm 31 and has a title of its own, reported as "Of David. A song. A psalm." See the variant.

a: on a ten-string harp
p: The kinnor was a small hand lyre; the nevel a larger stringed instrument. "Ten" may describe either.
b: Literally "with a kinnor, with a nevel of ten (strings)". The kinnor was the lyre David played for Saul (1 Samuel 16:23), a wooden frame with strings, held in the arms. The nevel was probably a larger lyre or harp, perhaps with a sound box. Instruments like both appear in Egyptian and Canaanite art and on Jewish coins of the Bar Kokhba revolt (AD 132–135). "Ten-stringed" may describe the nevel (as in 144:9) or be a third instrument (92:3).

a: Sing him a new song
p: The "new song" answers a new act of God. Revelation hears the redeemed sing one before the throne.
b: The phrase appears here first, then in 40:3, 96:1, 98:1, 144:9, 149:1 and Isaiah 42:10. A new song may be a song for a fresh act of rescue, or a new performance of the old praise. In Revelation the living creatures and elders, and then the 144,000, sing a new song to the Lamb (Revelation 5:9; Revelation 14:3).

a: the LORD's word is upright
p: Verses 4–5 name God's word and work, and verses 6–9 tell how the word made the world.
b: The psalm moves from God's speech (davar) to his deeds (ma'aseh), and the rest of the poem unfolds both: the word that made the heavens (33:6–9) and the plan that rules history (33:10–12). "Upright" (yashar) means straight, honest, not bent. "In faithfulness" (be'emunah) means reliably.

a: The heavens were made by the LORD's word
p: The verse sums up Genesis 1: God speaks, and it is. Christians read in it the Word and the Spirit.
b: Like Genesis 1, the verse says God made the sky by speaking, and verse 9 echoes the refrain "and it was so". "Breath" (ruach) is also "spirit" or "wind" (Genesis 1:2). Jewish tradition counts the ten sayings of creation in Genesis 1 (Mishnah Avot 5:1). Early Christian writers such as Irenaeus (Demonstration of the Apostolic Preaching 5) read "word" and "breath" as the Son and the Spirit at work in creation, and linked the verse with John 1:1–3. Jewish readers answer that the verse is a poetic pair: word and breath of mouth are one act of speech.

a: all their starry army
p: Tseva'am, "their host", means the stars, the same word as in the title "the LORD of Armies".
b: Tsava' is an army. "The host of heaven" is the stars (Genesis 2:1; Deuteronomy 4:19; Isaiah 40:26), which other nations worshiped as gods. Here they are simply things God made by speaking. The divine title "the LORD of Armies" uses the same word; see 24:10.

a: like a mound
p: The Hebrew vowels say "like a heap" (as at the Red Sea); the Greek and others read "like a wineskin".
b: Kanned means "like a heap" or "wall" of water, the word used when the sea stood up at the crossing (Exodus 15:8; Psalm 78:13; Joshua 3:13). The same consonants with other vowels, kanod, mean "like a skin bottle", and the Greek (askon), Latin, Targum and Syriac read it that way. Both pictures work: God either piles up the sea or bottles it up, and the next line says he stores it in storehouses. See the variant.

a: the people he chose as his own inheritance
p: Verse 12 is about Israel; Christian readers have also applied it to the church and, often, to their own nations.
b: "The nation whose God is the LORD" is Israel, chosen as God's nachalah, his inheritance or family property (Deuteronomy 32:9; Exodus 19:5–6). Jewish liturgy uses the verse in that sense. Christians have read it of the church (compare 1 Peter 2:9). The verse has also been quoted for modern nations, especially in American public speech, a use most commentators say goes beyond the psalm, which names one people and one God.

a: He shapes the hearts of them all
p: Yachad means "together" or "alike". The verb is the potter's verb from Genesis 2:7.
b: Hayyotser, "the one who shapes", is the verb for the potter and for God forming Adam from clay (Genesis 2:7; Jeremiah 18:6). Yachad can mean "together" (he formed every heart) or "alike" (he made them all the same way, KJV). The point is that the maker of hearts knows what is in them.

a: The horse is a lie when you hope for victory
p: Horses and chariots were the tanks of the ancient world, and Israel's law warned the king not to pile them up.
b: Egypt, Assyria and the Canaanite cities fought with chariot corps. Deuteronomy 17:16 tells Israel's king not to collect horses, and Solomon broke the rule (1 Kings 10:26–29). Psalm 20:7 sets trusting in chariots and horses against trusting in God's name, and Isaiah 31:1 condemns those who go down to Egypt for horses. This verse belongs to the same protest: safety is not in the size of an army (33:16).

a: We wait for the LORD with all our being
p: Nafshenu, "our soul", is the whole living self. The Plain says "with all our being".
b: Nefesh is the whole person, throat, life and self, not a soul separate from the body. "Our soul waits" (KJV) means we wait with everything in us. Chikkah, "wait", is a patient, expectant waiting.

a: in front of Abimelech
p: 1 Samuel 21 names the king of Gath Achish. The title says Abimelech, perhaps a royal title.
b: The title points to 1 Samuel 21:10–15, where David, on the run from Saul, fled to Achish king of Gath and "in front of them he hid his good sense, and in their grip he played the madman" (1 Samuel 21:13). The title uses the same rare phrase, "changed his sense" (shinnah et-ta'mo), but names the king Abimelech. Explanations: Abimelech ("my father is king") was a title for Philistine kings, as "Pharaoh" was for Egypt's (compare Genesis 20; 26); the title-writer confused two stories; or the title preserves a different tradition. Critical scholars note that nothing in the psalm itself mentions madness or Gath.

a: when he changed his behavior
p: Shinnah et-ta'mo is literally "changed his taste", the same word as "taste and see" in 34:8.
b: Ta'am means taste, and so judgment or good sense. David "changed his taste" when he faked madness; the psalm then calls on the hearer to "taste (ta'amu) and see" (34:8). Many readers think the title-writer chose this story because of the shared word, a common way ancient scribes linked psalms to David's life.

a: At every time I will bless the LORD
p: Psalm 34 is an acrostic: each verse starts with the next Hebrew letter, with waw missing and an extra pe.
b: Verse 1 starts with alef, verse 2 with bet, and so on to tav in verse 21. There is no verse for waw (the sixth letter; some find it hidden in the second half of 34:5, which begins with waw), and verse 22 is an extra line beginning with pe, outside the alphabet. Psalm 25 has a similar shape: it also lacks waw (and qof), and it also ends with an extra pe line. Some scholars note that the first, middle and last lines (alef 34:1, lamed 34:11, pe 34:22) together spell alef, from a root meaning "learn" or "teach". English cannot show the alphabet, so the chapter page lists the letters.

a: let the lowly hear and rejoice
p: 'Anavim are the poor and humble, people with no power to defend themselves. They are the psalm's audience.
b: 'Anavim (from a root meaning to be bent low) are the lowly: poor, oppressed, and therefore humble before God. The psalm is addressed to them (34:2, 6, 18). The same word stands behind "the humble will take possession of the land" (37:11), which Jesus takes up in Matthew 5:5.

a: They looked to him and their faces shone
p: Naharu means to beam with light. The Greek and Syriac make it a command: "Look to him and be lit up."
b: Nahar is used of a face lighting up with joy (Isaiah 60:5). The Masoretic Text has the past tense ("they looked ... and shone ... their faces"). The Greek, Syriac and Jerome read commands: "Look to him and be radiant, and your faces will not be ashamed" (the Greek has "come near to him"). The change is a matter of vowels and one letter. See the variant.

a: Here was a poor man who called out
p: "This poor man" is probably the poet himself, pointing to his own story as proof.
b: Literally "this poor one called". The psalmist points at himself, the case the humble (34:2) can look at. Readers who follow the title take it as David at Gath. The Midrash on Psalms tells that David had once asked God why he made madness, and was answered when feigned madness saved his life at Gath.

a: The angel of the LORD pitches camp around those who fear him
p: The picture is of an army camped around the faithful. The angel of the LORD appears only twice in Psalms.
b: The angel of the LORD appears in the psalms only here and in 35:5–6. The image may recall Jacob's vision of God's camp at Mahanaim (Genesis 32:1–2) or Elisha's hills full of fiery horses (2 Kings 6:17). Jewish and Christian readers have found here the idea of guardian angels (compare 91:11; Matthew 18:10; Hebrews 1:14). Some Christian interpreters identify the angel of the LORD with the Son of God before his birth; others, and Jewish readers, see God's messenger.

a: Taste and see: the LORD is good!
p: 1 Peter 2:3 borrows the line for new believers, and the early church sang Psalm 34 at communion.
b: First Peter tells new Christians to crave spiritual milk, "if you have tasted that the Lord is good" (1 Peter 2:3, a fresh rendering), taking the Greek of this verse (chrēstos ho kyrios). By the 300s, Psalm 34 was sung while people received communion: Cyril of Jerusalem tells the newly baptized that they hear the singer invite them, "Taste and see that the Lord is good". The Orthodox liturgy of the Presanctified Gifts still uses it as the communion hymn. In the psalm itself the tasting is of God's goodness in rescue.

a: Young lions run short and go hungry
p: Kefirim are young lions, the strongest hunters. The Greek reads "the rich", perhaps from a similar word.
b: Even the lions, which take what they want by force, sometimes go hungry; those who seek God do not lack what is good. The Greek has "the rich have become poor and gone hungry" (plousioi), and the Syriac agrees. The translator may have read a word for "great ones" or treated the lions as a picture of the powerful (as in 35:17). The closing verses of the Jewish grace after meals include 34:9–10 and 37:25.

a: Come here, children, and hear me out
p: From verse 11 the psalm turns from thanks to teaching, like a wisdom teacher with pupils.
b: "Children" (banim, sons) is how a wisdom teacher addresses students (Proverbs 1:8; 4:1). "The fear of the LORD" is the beginning of wisdom in Proverbs (Proverbs 1:7; 9:10). The second half of the psalm reads like a lesson: who wants life? Here is how to live it. Scholars call Psalm 34 a thanksgiving that becomes a wisdom psalm.

a: Is there anyone who wants life
p: 1 Peter 3:10–12 quotes 34:12–16 from the Greek to teach Christians how to answer abuse.
b: First Peter quotes verses 12–16a: "Whoever wants to love life and see good days must keep his tongue from evil and his lips from speaking deceit. He must turn from evil and do good, seek peace and pursue it. For the eyes of the Lord are on the righteous and his ears toward their prayer, but the face of the Lord is against those who do evil" (1 Peter 3:10–12, a fresh rendering). Peter stops before "to wipe their memory from the earth", leaving room for the persecutors to change. He applies it to Christians who are slandered: do not pay back insult for insult.

a: look for peace and run after it
p: The rabbis made this verse a rule: other commands you keep when they come to you; peace you must chase.
b: Baqqesh shalom verodfehu: seek it and pursue it. A saying in the midrash (Leviticus Rabbah 9:9) notes that the Torah says "if you happen on" for other duties, but here says "pursue": peace must be run after. Hillel's saying in Mishnah Avot 1:12 urges people to be like the disciples of Aaron, "loving peace and pursuing peace".

a: Near to the broken-hearted is the LORD
p: "Broken of heart" and "crushed of spirit" are people shattered by suffering, not just people who feel sorry.
b: The words describe people crushed by suffering or loss, not mainly the sorry heart of repentance (though 51:17 uses similar words for that). Isaiah 57:15 and 61:1 promise that God lives with the crushed and lowly and binds up the broken-hearted.

a: not a single one gets broken
p: John 19:36 says Jesus' legs were not broken to fulfill Scripture: this verse, the Passover law, or both.
b: When the soldiers did not break Jesus' legs, John writes: "These things happened so that the Scripture would be fulfilled: Not one of his bones will be broken" (John 19:36, a fresh rendering). He may cite the Passover rule, "do not break any of its bones" (Exodus 12:46; compare Numbers 9:12), so that Jesus is the true Passover lamb, or this psalm's promise for the righteous sufferer, or both. John's verb, "will be broken", matches the Greek of this psalm; his "bone" matches Exodus. In the psalm the line means God protects the righteous body, not that the righteous never suffer (34:19).

a: The LORD buys back the lives of his servants
p: This last verse begins with pe, after the alphabet has ended at tav. It turns the curse of verse 21 into a promise.
b: Verse 21 (tav) ends the alphabet with the wicked condemned. Verse 22 adds a line that begins with podeh, "buys back, ransoms", the verb for redeeming a firstborn or a slave (Exodus 13:13; Deuteronomy 7:8). The poem refuses to end on judgment. "Will be found guilty" (ye'shemu) is the same verb in both verses.

a: take up my case
p: Riv is a lawsuit. The psalm mixes the courtroom (35:1, 11, 23–24) with the battlefield (35:1–3).
b: Rivah YHWH et-yerivai: "contend, LORD, with those who contend with me", a legal term (as in Isaiah 3:13; Micah 6:1–2). The second line moves to war, and verses 2–3 arm God with shields and spear. Later the poet faces false witnesses (35:11) and asks God to wake up and judge (35:23–24). Many scholars think the setting is a man falsely accused, perhaps in a trial at the temple (compare 1 Kings 8:31–32).

a: the battle-axe
t: Close the way, or the axe?
p: Segor may be a verb, "block the way" (KJV), or a weapon, the double axe called sagaris in Greek.
b: The Masoretic vowels make segor an imperative, "and close (the way)", so the KJV supplies "stop the way against them". The Greek also has "shut in". But a weapon fits the list (shield, buckler, spear), and many scholars connect the word with sagaris, a battle-axe used by Scythians and Persians. The Plain follows the weapon reading, as most modern versions do.

a: Let those who are after my life
p: Psalm 35 is one of the curse psalms. It asks God, not the poet, to defeat the enemies.
b: Verses 4–8 and 26 ask that the attackers be shamed, scattered and caught in their own nets. The poet does not plan revenge; he puts his case in God's hands. Jewish and Christian readers have handled such lines in very different ways (see the chapter page). Verse 4 is almost the same as 40:14 and 70:2.

a: the LORD's angel
p: The angel who camps around the faithful in 34:7 here chases their enemies.
b: The two psalms are placed side by side and share the angel: in 34:7 he guards, in 35:5–6 he drives the attackers like chaff and chases them down a dark, slippery path. The picture recalls the angel who went before Israel against its enemies (Exodus 23:20–23) and the angel who struck the Assyrian camp (2 Kings 19:35).

a: they hid their net for me
p: The Hebrew reads "they hid for me the pit of their net"; most scholars move one word to the next line.
b: Literally "for no reason they hid for me the pit of their net; for no reason they dug for my life". The second line lacks an object and the first has two. Moving "pit" (shachat) to the second line gives the neat pair the Plain prints: they hid a net; they dug a pit. No manuscript moves the word, and the Greek keeps the Hebrew order ("destruction of their trap"). The variant gives the Masoretic order.

a: I am left like a parent robbed of children
p: Shekhol is the loss of children. The poet feels as alone as parents whose children have died.
b: Shekhol lenafshi, "bereavement to my soul". Shakal is the word for losing children (Genesis 27:45; 43:14). Some scholars emend slightly to "they lie in wait for my soul". The Plain keeps the Hebrew.

a: my prayer kept coming back to my own chest
p: He prayed with head bowed to his chest; or the prayer went unanswered; or its blessing came back on him.
b: Literally "my prayer returned to my bosom". (1) It describes posture: he prayed bent over, head on chest (compare Elijah, 1 Kings 18:42). (2) The prayer was unanswered and came back to him. (3) The good he wished them, they refused, so it came back to him as a blessing (compare Matthew 10:13, "let your peace return to you"). The Greek simply translates the words. The point of the verse is clear: he fasted and mourned for these men when they were sick.

a: the beaten-down gathered against me
p: Nekhim may mean "smitten ones" (outcasts, KJV "abjects") or "smiters". Some emend to "strangers".
b: Nekhim comes from nakhah, "strike". As a passive it would be "stricken people", the lowest of society (KJV "the abjects"); some read "those who strike", or emend to nokhrim, "foreigners". The Greek has "whips" (mastiges), and gathers twice. Verses 15–16 are among the hardest Hebrew in the Psalter, and every English version guesses.

a: Like godless men who mock for a cake of bread
p: Literally "with the godless of mockers of a cake": perhaps hangers-on who jeer for a free meal.
b: Ma'og is a round cake of bread (1 Kings 17:12). One explanation: hangers-on who will mock anyone for a free meal, the KJV's "hypocritical mockers in feasts". Others emend to "they mocked me with mocking", close to what the Greek has ("they tested me, they sneered at me with sneering"). Whatever the exact words, the picture is of a jeering crowd grinding their teeth.

a: my only life
p: Yechidati, "my only one", is the poet's own life, his one precious possession. The same word stands in 22:20.
b: Yachid is "only", the word for an only child (Genesis 22:2, Isaac). Here and in 22:20 it means one's own life, the one thing a person cannot replace (KJV "my darling").

a: do not let those who hate me for no reason
p: Jesus says, "They hated me for no reason" (John 15:25), citing "their law". The words match this verse and 69:4.
b: In John 15:25 Jesus explains the world's hatred: it happened "so that the word written in their law would be fulfilled: They hated me for no reason" (a fresh rendering). "Law" there means the Scriptures as a whole. The phrase "those who hate me for no reason" (sone'ai chinnam) appears in this verse and in 69:4 (compare 109:3; 119:161). Christians read the righteous sufferer of these psalms as a pattern fulfilled in Jesus; Jewish readers hear the voice of David and of any innocent person or of Israel among the nations.

a: wink at me
p: A wink was a sign of mockery or plotting, as in Proverbs: someone who winks is up to no good.
b: Qarats 'ayin, to narrow the eye, is a gesture of malice or secret plotting in Proverbs (Proverbs 6:13; 10:10; 16:30). The enemies share a knowing look over the poet's downfall.

a: the quiet people of the land
p: Rig'ei-erets, a phrase found only here: peaceable people who do not fight back.
b: Rig'ei-erets are the peaceful, those who live quietly and make no trouble. The enemies plot against exactly the people least able to defend themselves.

a: my God and my Lord
p: Thomas's confession in John 20:28 uses the same pair in the other order.
b: Elohai wa'donai: "my God and my Lord". Thomas, seeing the risen Jesus, says "My Lord and my God" (John 20:28, Greek ho kyrios mou kai ho theos mou). The Greek of this verse has ho theos mou kai ho kyrios mou. Some commentators on John suggest he echoes the psalm's language for God; others think the pairing was simply common.

a: who takes pleasure in his servant's well-being
p: Shalom is welfare, wholeness and safety. The God who delights in it is the reason the friends can shout.
b: Shelom 'avdo: the shalom of his servant. Shalom covers health, safety, prosperity and right relations. The psalm ends where it began, in court (35:23–24): those who "want me proved right" (literally "who delight in my righteousness") will celebrate when God gives the verdict.

a: the LORD's servant
p: Only Psalms 18 and 36 give David the title "servant of the LORD" in their headings.
b: The title 'eved YHWH belongs to Moses (Deuteronomy 34:5; Joshua 1:1), Joshua (Joshua 24:29) and David (2 Samuel 7:5; Psalm 89:3). Among psalm titles it occurs only here and in 18:0. Some see in it a mark of a royal collection; others think it fits a psalm about the man who serves God against the man whom rebellion addresses (36:1).

a: Rebellion speaks like a prophet to the wicked
p: Ne'um, "oracle" or "utterance", is the prophets' word for a message from God. Here Rebellion is the speaker.
b: Ne'um nearly always introduces God's speech: "says the LORD" (ne'um YHWH), hundreds of times in the prophets. Here the speaker is pesha', rebellion, as if sin were a false god giving its oracle to its worshiper. The line is a dark parody of prophecy. Its Hebrew is famously hard: the KJV has "the transgression of the wicked saith within my heart".

a: He has no dread of God
p: Paul ends his chain of Scripture quotations in Romans 3 with this line.
b: Romans 3:10–18 strings together lines from the Psalms and Isaiah to show that all, Jew and Greek, are under sin. It ends with this verse: "There is no fear of God before their eyes" (Romans 3:18, a fresh rendering). The word here is pachad, dread or terror, not the usual yir'ah.

a: too smoothly to find his guilt and hate it
p: Literally "for he makes it smooth to him in his eyes, to find his guilt, to hate". Who flatters whom is unclear.
b: The subject may be the wicked man (he flatters himself, so he never finds and hates his sin), or Rebellion from verse 1 (it flatters him until his guilt is found out and hated, so the KJV). The Greek has "for he dealt deceitfully before him, to find his lawlessness and hate it". All readings agree on the main point: self-deceit keeps the wicked from facing his sin.

a: Lying in bed, he works out trouble
p: The bed is the place for reflection and prayer (4:4; 63:6). The wicked use it to plan harm.
b: Micah 2:1 says the same of land-grabbers: "Woe to those who plan trouble and work out evil on their beds; at morning light they do it" (a fresh rendering; Micah is not yet translated on this site). The faithful lie awake meditating on God (4:4; 63:6); the wicked lie awake scheming.

a: the mountains of God
p: "Of God" (El) can work as a superlative: the mightiest mountains. It may also mean the gods' mountain of old myth.
b: Hebrew can use "God" to mean "very great": "cedars of God" (80:10) are huge cedars, "a mountain of God" a vast one (68:15). So "mountains of God" may simply be the highest mountains (BSB). Some hear more: the mountain where God lives (Exodus 3:1; Ezekiel 28:14), as the next line names "the great deep" (tehom rabbah), the waters below the earth (Genesis 7:11). God's righteousness reaches from top to bottom of the world.

a: in the shadow of your wings
p: The image may be of a mother bird, or of the cherub wings over the ark in the temple.
b: Ruth comes to take shelter under the LORD's wings (Ruth 2:12), and Jesus longs to gather Jerusalem like a hen gathers her chicks (Matthew 23:37). Many scholars also see the temple here: the cherubim spread their wings over the atonement lid (1 Kings 8:6–7), and the next verse speaks of feasting in God's house. The phrase recurs in 17:8, 57:1, 61:4, 63:7 and 91:4.

a: your river of delights
p: "Delights" is 'adanekha, the same root as Eden. God's house is pictured as a garden with a river.
b: Nachal 'adanekha is literally "the stream of your delights" or "of your Edens". Eden means delight, and from Eden a river flowed out to water the garden (Genesis 2:10). The temple is pictured as paradise with its river, as in 46:4, Ezekiel 47:1–12 and Revelation 22:1–2. "Rich food" (deshen, fatness) is the feast of the sacrificial meal.

a: in your light we see light
p: A short line with a long history: in the Trinity debates, in John's Gospel and as a university motto.
b: In context, God's light is his favor and life: in his presence people see clearly and live. Gregory of Nazianzus (Oration 31.3) and Basil read it of the Trinity: in the light of the Spirit we see the Son, who is "light from light", as the Nicene Creed says. John's Gospel joins "life" and "light" as this verse does (John 1:4; 8:12). The Latin, in lumine tuo videbimus lumen, is the motto of Columbia University.

a: Do not burn up inside over people who do evil
p: Tit-char is literally "heat yourself up". The same command comes three times (37:1, 7, 8).
b: Al-titchar is from charah, "to burn", the word for anger. "Fret" (KJV) is gentler than the Hebrew: do not let it make you hot with rage or envy. Proverbs 24:19 has almost the same line. The Talmud asks how this fits other verses that tell the righteous to oppose the wicked, and answers that it speaks to a person whose own conscience is not clear (Berakhot 7b).

a: Do not burn up inside
p: Psalm 37 is an acrostic: every other verse, roughly, begins with the next letter of the alphabet.
b: Most letters get two verses: alef 37:1–2, bet 37:3–4, gimel 37:5–6, and so on to tav 37:39–40. A few letters have one verse or three. In the Masoretic Text the ayin line is missing at 37:28; a Qumran commentary and the Greek preserve it (see the variant there). The alphabet suits a teaching poem meant to be memorized. The chapter page lists the letters.

a: graze on faithfulness
p: Re'eh 'emunah can mean "graze safely", "feed on faithfulness", or "befriend faithfulness".
b: Ra'ah is to pasture or graze (and also, with different vowels, to befriend). 'Emunah is faithfulness or security. So: "feed on faithfulness", "enjoy safe pasture", or "cultivate faithfulness" (BSB). The KJV's "verily thou shalt be fed" takes 'emunah as an adverb. The Plain keeps the farming picture of the land that runs through the psalm.

a: Roll your way onto the LORD
p: Gol is "roll", as a load is rolled off one's back. Proverbs 16:3 has the same picture.
b: Gol 'al-YHWH darkekha. The verb galal is to roll a stone or a burden (Genesis 29:3). The same idiom is in 22:8 and Proverbs 16:3. "Commit" (KJV) is right in sense; the Hebrew is more vivid. 1 Peter 5:7 says something similar with a different verb ("throw all your worry on him").

a: will take possession of the land
p: Yarash ha'arets is the Bible's phrase for taking the promised land. It occurs five times here (37:9, 11, 22, 29, 34).
b: "Take possession of the land" is the language of Deuteronomy and Joshua: Israel entering Canaan. Psalm 37 promises the land not to the strong but to those who wait, the humble, the blessed, the righteous, and those who keep God's way. Erets can mean the land (of Israel) or the earth; the Greek has gē, which can mean either, and so Matthew 5:5 promises the humble "the earth". See the note at 37:11.

a: But the humble will take possession of the land
p: Jesus' beatitude "Happy are the humble, for they will inherit the earth" (Matthew 5:5) takes up this verse.
b: Matthew 5:5 is very close to the Greek of this verse (hoi de praeis klēronomēsousin gēn). "Meek" in older English meant gentle, not weak; the Hebrew 'anavim are the poor and lowly who depend on God (see 34:2). Whether the promise means the land of Israel, the whole earth, or a renewed creation is debated (see the chapter page). A Qumran commentary on this psalm (4Q171) applies it to "the congregation of the poor", their own community.

a: The Lord laughs at him
p: God's laughter is not cruelty but certainty: he sees the end the wicked cannot see.
b: God laughs at the plotting rulers of 2:4 and at the nations in 59:8. The laugh says that the threat is not as large as it looks from below. The wicked man's "day" is the day of his judgment or death (compare 1 Samuel 26:10).

a: The little that a righteous person has is better
p: A "better than" saying, the classic form of Proverbs. Jesus and Paul both repeat the thought.
b: Proverbs 15:16 and 16:8 have the same form: better a little with the fear of the LORD than great treasure with trouble. Compare 1 Timothy 6:6–8 and Luke 12:15.

a: like the splendor of the fields
p: Kiqar karim can be "like the glory of the pastures" or "like the fat of lambs" (KJV), burned up on the altar.
b: Karim means both "pastures" and "lambs"; yeqar is preciousness or splendor. The KJV reads "as the fat of lambs", which burns up in smoke on the altar, and that fits the next words, "they vanish like smoke". Most modern versions read "pastures", like the grass of 37:2. The Greek has "as soon as they are honored and exalted, they vanish like smoke". Either way, their glory is brief.

a: The wicked man takes a loan and never repays
p: In a farming village, lending to a neighbor in a bad year was a duty, and interest from the poor was forbidden.
b: The law told Israelites to lend to the poor without interest (Exodus 22:25; Deuteronomy 15:7–11). Psalm 37 measures righteousness by how a person handles money in hard times: the wicked man takes and does not repay, the righteous man gives (37:26; compare 112:5).

a: I was a young man, and now I am old too
p: An old man's testimony. Readers ask how it fits the suffering of the righteous in Job and other psalms.
b: The speaker sounds like an elder teaching from experience. Many readers find the claim too simple: Job, Psalm 44 and Psalm 73 complain that the righteous do suffer. Answers given: the verse is a general rule, as proverbs are; "left on his own" means left by God for good, not never needy; or the righteous man's children are cared for by a community that lends (37:26). The Jewish grace after meals ends with this verse among others (with 34:9–10); many people say it quietly, out of tact toward anyone at the table who is in need.

a: The mouth of the righteous murmurs wisdom
p: Hagah is the low murmur of reading aloud or meditating, the word of 1:2.
b: Yehgeh is the same verb used of meditating on the law day and night in 1:2, and of the coo of a dove (Isaiah 38:14). The next verse explains where the wisdom comes from: the law of God in the heart (37:31; compare Deuteronomy 6:6; Jeremiah 31:33).

a: like a lush tree in its native soil
p: Ezrach ra'anan is a "leafy native", a tree that has never been moved. The Greek has "the cedars of Lebanon".
b: Ezrach is the word for a native-born citizen (Exodus 12:19); here it is a tree grown in its own soil and firmly rooted. The KJV's "green bay tree" is a guess. The Greek reads hōs tas kedrous tou Libanou, "like the cedars of Lebanon", which suggests a Hebrew ke'erez levanon (similar letters). See the variant.

a: for the man of peace has a future
p: 'Acharit is the "afterward": a future, descendants, a good end. The wicked have none (37:38).
b: 'Acharit can mean the end of a life, what comes after, or posterity. The KJV reads "the end of that man is peace". Most modern scholars read "there is a future (or posterity) for the man of peace", set against 37:38, "the future of the wicked will be cut off". Some Jewish and Christian readers have found here a hint of life after death; most scholars see descendants and a good name.

a: To bring to remembrance.
p: Lehazkir may tie the psalm to the 'azkarah, the token portion burned with incense, or simply mean "to remind God".
b: Lehazkir ("to cause to remember") stands in the titles of Psalms 38 and 70 only. Three explanations: (1) it marks a psalm sung with the 'azkarah, the token portion of a grain offering burned on the altar (Leviticus 2:2; 24:7); (2) it is a prayer meant to remind God of the sufferer (compare Isaiah 62:6); (3) the Levites were appointed "to call him to mind, to give thanks, and to praise" (1 Chronicles 16:4; "call to mind" is the same verb). The Greek adds "concerning the Sabbath"; see the variant.

a: LORD, not in your fury, do not rebuke me
p: The first line is almost the same as 6:1. Both are among the seven penitential psalms.
b: Psalm 6:1 opens with the same Hebrew except for one word (qetsef "rage" here, 'af "anger" there in the first line). The poet does not ask to escape discipline altogether, only discipline given in fury (compare Jeremiah 10:24). From Cassiodorus in the 500s, the church counted Psalms 6, 32, 38, 51, 102, 130 and 143 as the seven penitential psalms, prayed in Lent and on Fridays.

a: my sin has left no peace in my bones
p: The poet links his illness with his sin. Other psalms and Job deny that every illness is a punishment.
b: Like many people in the ancient world, the speaker believes his sickness is God's discipline for sin (38:3–5, 18). The Bible keeps this belief alongside its denials: Job is sick but blameless (Job 2:3–7), and Jesus refuses to say a blind man's sin caused his blindness (John 9:2–3). Readers differ on whether the psalm teaches a rule or voices one sufferer's honest reading of his own case. Either way, the prayer does not argue: it confesses and asks.

a: because I was a fool
p: Iwwelet is moral folly in Proverbs: the fool's refusal to learn, not low intelligence.
b: Iwwelet is the folly of the ewil, the fool of Proverbs who despises wisdom (Proverbs 1:7; 5:23). Here the poet calls his sin folly, the same self-judgment as 69:5.

a: For my loins are full of scorching pain
p: Kesalim are the loins or lower back; niqleh is "burning" or "inflammation". The KJV's "loathsome disease" is a guess.
b: Kesalai mal'u niqleh: "my loins are full of what is roasted" or "burning". The illness is not named. Some have guessed a fever or an inflamed wound; the KJV's "loathsome disease" reads the word as "despised". The psalm uses the language of illness, whether literal or a picture of deep distress.

a: keep their distance from the blow that struck me
p: Luke may echo this verse when he says Jesus' friends "stood at a distance" at the cross.
b: Nega', "blow, stroke" (the same word as "your blow" in 39:10), is the word used for the skin disease that kept people outside the camp (Leviticus 13:3), so the friends may be keeping away for fear of uncleanness or bad luck. Luke 23:49 says all who knew Jesus "stood at a distance" watching, with words close to the Greek of this verse (apo makrothen estēsan). Job also complains that his relatives have left him (Job 19:13–14).

a: like a man who cannot speak, I keep my mouth shut
p: The sufferer does not answer his accusers. Christians link the line with Isaiah 53:7 and Jesus' silence at his trial.
b: The poet leaves his defense to God (38:15). Isaiah's servant "did not open his mouth" like a lamb led to slaughter (Isaiah 53:7), and the Gospels show Jesus silent before the high priest and Pilate (Matthew 26:63; Matthew 27:12–14). Psalm 39 picks up the same silence (39:2, 9).

a: But my enemies are alive and strong
p: The Hebrew reads chayyim, "alive". A Qumran scroll and many scholars read chinnam, "for no reason", as in 35:19.
b: Literally "my enemies, living, are strong". The parallel line has "those who hate me falsely" (sheqer), and 35:19 and 69:4 pair the same two words: enemies who "lie" (sheqer) and "those who hate me for no reason" (chinnam). The scroll 4QPs-a is reported to read chinnam here, though only its last letters are clear, and many scholars adopt it. The Greek has "my enemies live", and Jerome and the Targum agree. The Plain follows the Masoretic Text; see the variant.

a: Lord, my salvation
p: Christians read Psalm 38 as Christ bearing others' sins. Jewish tradition hears David or Israel.
b: Augustine reads the psalm in the voice of the whole Christ, head and body: the sins confessed belong to the members, and Christ makes them his own. Medieval commentators linked 38:11 and 38:13 with the passion. Jewish interpreters such as Rashi and Radak read it as David's prayer in illness, or as the voice of Israel in exile.

a: For Jeduthun.
p: Jeduthun was one of David's three chief Levite musicians, with Asaph and Heman. The Hebrew spells the name two ways.
b: Chronicles names Jeduthun with Asaph and Heman as leaders of the temple singers (1 Chronicles 16:41–42; 25:1–6; 2 Chronicles 5:12). He is perhaps the same man as Ethan (compare 1 Chronicles 15:17, 19 with 1 Chronicles 16:41). His name stands in the titles of Psalms 39, 62 and 77. "For Jeduthun" may mean the psalm was given to his guild, or (in 62 and 77, which say "according to Jeduthun") a style or tune. The written text (Ketiv) here spells him Jedithun; the reading tradition (Qere) says Jeduthun, the usual form.

a: My mouth will wear a muzzle
p: Machsom occurs only here: a muzzle for an animal. The poet does not trust himself to speak in front of the wicked.
b: Machsom, from chasam, "to muzzle" (Deuteronomy 25:4, the ox treading grain). He keeps quiet "as long as the wicked are in front of me": either because complaining would give the scoffers ammunition, or because he fears he would accuse God. The silence does not last (39:3).

a: though it did no good
p: Hecheshet mittov may mean "I kept silent, even from good words" (KJV), or "to no good", or "far from good".
b: Literally "I was silent from good". (1) He refused to speak even good words (KJV, "even from good"). (2) His silence was "to no avail": holding it in did no good (the Plain). (3) He was "far from happiness". The next words, "my pain was stirred up", support the second: silence only made it worse.

a: My heart was burning inside me
p: Jeremiah too could not keep silent: the word was like a fire shut up in his bones.
b: Compare Jeremiah 20:9: when the prophet tried not to speak, there was "in my heart like a burning fire shut up in my bones". On the road to Emmaus the disciples say, "Were not our hearts burning within us?" (Luke 24:32). Here the fire forces out not preaching but a question about the shortness of life.

a: LORD, show me my end
p: Not a request for the date of death, but to grasp how short life is. Brahms set these lines in his German Requiem.
b: The prayer asks God to make the poet feel his limits: life has an end and a measure. Psalm 90:12 asks similarly: "Teach us, then, to count our days". Johannes Brahms set 39:4–7 in Luther's German as the third movement of A German Requiem (1868): Herr, lehre doch mich, dass ein Ende mit mir haben muss. The Book of Common Prayer appointed Psalm 39 (with Psalm 90) for the burial of the dead.

a: you have made my days handbreadths
p: The tefach was the width of four fingers, about 3 inches (7.5 cm), the smallest common measure.
b: Builders measured by the cubit (the forearm, about 18 inches) and the handbreadth (one sixth of a cubit). The temple sea was a handbreadth thick (1 Kings 7:26). A life measured in handbreadths is a very short thing.

a: is nothing but a puff of air
p: Hevel is breath or vapor, the key word of Ecclesiastes ("Breath of breaths"). It returns in 39:6 and 39:11.
b: Hevel is the breath you see on a cold morning, there and gone. Ecclesiastes uses it 38 times ("vanity of vanities" in the KJV). Job says "my days are a puff of air" (Job 7:16), and the name Abel (Hevel) belongs to the man whose life was cut short (Genesis 4:2, 8). "Even standing firm" (nitstsav) means even at his strongest, a man is only breath.

a: only a shadow-shape
p: Tselem, "image", is the word of Genesis 1:27. Here it is a mere outline, a shadow-figure.
b: Betselem yithallekh-ish, "as an image a man walks about". Tselem is the "image" of God in Genesis 1:26–27, but in 73:20 it is a dream-figure that vanishes on waking. The poet sees people as shadow-shapes, busy and noisy, piling up wealth for someone else (compare Luke 12:20; Ecclesiastes 2:18–19).

a: like a moth you melt away what he holds dear
p: Moths eat away cloth, the ancient world's stored wealth. Jesus uses the same picture.
b: Fine clothing was a way to store wealth. The moth ruins it quietly from inside (Job 13:28; Isaiah 50:9). Jesus warns against treasure on earth, "where moth and rust destroy" (Matthew 6:19, a fresh rendering).

a: For I am a foreigner with you
p: Ger and toshav are the legal words for a resident foreigner and a lodger. Israel lives on God's land as his guest.
b: Abraham called himself "a foreigner ... and a settler" among the Hittites (Genesis 23:4). God says of the land, "You are foreigners and lodgers living with me" (Leviticus 25:23), and David prays, "we are foreigners before you, and lodgers, as all our fathers were" (1 Chronicles 29:15), almost this line. A ger had protection but no land of his own and depended on the host's kindness. The poet asks God to treat him as a host treats a guest. Hebrews 11:13 and 1 Peter 2:11 call believers foreigners and exiles on earth.

a: before I go away and am no more
p: The psalm ends with no hope stated beyond death. Readers differ on what that silence means.
b: "Take your eyes off me" (hasha', look away) is Job's prayer too (Job 7:19; 10:20; 14:6): God's watching gaze feels like a weight. "Am no more" may mean simply death, as in Job 7:21. Many scholars see here the older Israelite view that the dead go silent to Sheol (6:5). Others note that the poet still speaks to God, and that later psalms and prophets went further (16:10; 49:15; Daniel 12:2). The Greek has "let me go, so that I may be refreshed".

a: I waited and waited for the LORD
p: Qavvoh qivviti doubles the verb: "waiting, I waited". Mendelssohn and U2 both set this opening.
b: Hebrew repeats a verb for emphasis. Qavah is to wait with hope, as a cord is stretched taut (the noun tiqvah means both "cord" and "hope"). Felix Mendelssohn set the line in his Lobgesang (1840), and the Irish band U2 sang verses 1–3 as their song "40" (1983).

a: out of the roaring pit
p: Bor sha'on, "pit of noise" or "of ruin". A cistern of mud, like the one Jeremiah sank in.
b: Sha'on is a roar or tumult, like rushing water, and may also mean desolation. The pit is a dry cistern with mud at the bottom, the kind Joseph was thrown into (Genesis 37:24) and Jeremiah sank in (Jeremiah 38:6). In the psalms the pit is also a name for the grave (28:1; 30:3). The rock is its opposite: firm ground.

a: He gave my mouth a new song
p: The rescue is not private: "many will see". Thanksgiving was sung in public at the temple.
b: Thanksgiving psalms tell the story of a rescue before the congregation, often with a thank offering (Leviticus 7:12–15; Psalm 116:17–19). Here the poet's song is a witness: others will see and trust. The "new song" is also in 33:3. Verses 1–10 are a thanksgiving; verses 11–17 a lament. Many scholars think two psalms were joined, since 40:13–17 appears alone as Psalm 70; others read the shift as deliberate: past rescue gives courage for new trouble.

a: the arrogant
p: Rehavim, "proud ones", is related to Rahab, the name of the sea monster and of Egypt.
b: Rehavim appears only here, from rahav, "to storm, to be arrogant". Rahab is the chaos monster God defeated (89:10; Job 26:12) and a poetic name for Egypt (87:4; Isaiah 30:7). Turning to the proud may mean trusting in great powers, or in false gods, "those who drift off after lies".

a: Sacrifice and grain offering you did not want
p: Like the prophets, the psalm puts obedience above offerings. Readers differ on how far that goes.
b: The four words cover the whole system: animal sacrifice (zevach), grain offering (minchah, here perhaps any gift), burnt offering ('olah) and sin offering (chata'ah). Samuel told Saul that "listening is better than sacrifice" (1 Samuel 15:22), and the prophets say similar things (Hosea 6:6; Amos 5:21–24; Micah 6:6–8; Jeremiah 7:22–23; compare Psalm 50:8–15; Psalm 51:16–17). Most Jewish and Christian interpreters read these as "not this, but first this": offerings without obedience are worthless. Some critical scholars read a real rejection of sacrifice, at least by some circles in Israel. Hebrews 10 reads the verse as announcing the end of animal sacrifice in Christ's offering of himself.

a: ears you have dug for me
p: 'Oznayim karita li: literally "ears you have dug for me". It probably means God opened his ears to hear and obey.
b: Karah means to dig, as a pit or a well (7:15; 57:6; Genesis 26:25). God has "dug out" ears in the poet: made a channel so that his word gets through. Isaiah 50:5 says "the Lord GOD has opened my ear" in the same sense, and the contrast with sacrifice fits: God wants hearing, that is, obedience (1 Samuel 15:22). Some readers see the slave whose ear was pierced at the door to mark lifelong service (Exodus 21:6), but that law uses another verb (ratsa') and one ear, not two. The Greek translation behind Hebrews 10:5 reads "a body you prepared for me" instead. See the variant and the chapter page.

a: Burnt offering and sin offering you did not ask for.
p: Hebrews 10:5–7 quotes 40:6–8 from the Greek, "a body you prepared", as the words of Christ entering the world.
b: Hebrews 10:5–7: "So when he comes into the world, he says: Sacrifice and offering you did not want, but a body you prepared for me. In burnt offerings and sin offerings you took no pleasure. Then I said, 'Look, I have come (in the scroll of the book it is written about me) to do your will, O God'" (a fresh rendering). The writer then argues (Hebrews 10:8–10) that Christ "takes away the first in order to set up the second", and that "we have been made holy through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all". The word "body" carries his point: Christ's obedience was done in a body, and offered as a sacrifice. The other small changes Hebrews makes to the psalm are set out on the chapter page.

a: Look, I have come.
p: Hinneh-vati is a servant's answer to his master's call: "I am here, at your service."
b: "Look, I have come" is the reply of someone reporting for duty (compare 1 Samuel 3:4–8; Isaiah 6:8). Hebrews takes it as the Son's answer on entering the world (Hebrews 10:7, 9).

a: The scroll of the book has it written about me.
p: The law of Moses, the king's copy of it, a written vow, or God's book of a life: readers differ.
b: Bimgillat-sefer katuv 'alay can mean "it is written about me" or "it is prescribed for me". Proposals: (1) the Torah, which spells out what God wants of him (Jewish commentators often read it so; compare 40:8); (2) the king's own copy of the law (Deuteronomy 17:18–19), if the speaker is a king; (3) a written thank-offering vow brought to the temple; (4) God's heavenly book in which a life is recorded (139:16). Hebrews reads it as the Scriptures as a whole, which speak of Christ (compare Luke 24:27). Megillah is a rolled scroll; this is one of its earliest uses.

a: your law is in my very core
p: Literally "your law is in the middle of my insides": Jeremiah's new covenant promise in one voice.
b: Betokh me'ai, "in the midst of my inner parts". God promised a new covenant in which he would "put my law within them and write it on their hearts" (Jeremiah 31:33; compare Deuteronomy 6:6; Psalm 37:31). Here one person already says so. Torah is "law", but also "teaching" or "instruction". The Greek has "in the middle of my belly".

a: I have brought the good news of righteousness
p: Bissarti is "I have announced good news". The Greek uses euangelizō, the root of "gospel".
b: Bisser is the messenger's verb for good news, such as victory in battle (2 Samuel 18:19–20; Isaiah 40:9; Isaiah 52:7). The Greek translates euēngelisamēn, the verb the New Testament uses for preaching the gospel. Here the good news is God's righteousness, his saving faithfulness, told aloud in the temple gathering.

a: My guilty deeds have caught up with me
p: After thanksgiving comes confession and a new plea. Reading the psalm as Christ's voice must face this.
b: Readers who take the whole psalm as spoken by Christ (following Hebrews 10) have had to explain a confession of sin in his mouth. Augustine answers that Christ speaks for his body, the church, and takes its sins as his own. Others say Hebrews quotes only verses 6–8 and does not claim the whole psalm. Jewish interpreters read it as David's prayer, or Israel's, with both thanks and confession.

a: LORD, may it please you to rescue me!
p: Verses 13–17 appear again, with small changes, as Psalm 70. It was probably sung on its own.
b: Psalm 70 repeats 40:13–17 almost word for word, and the site's Plain uses the same English in both wherever the Hebrew is the same. The main differences: Psalm 70 uses "God" (Elohim) in some places where Psalm 40 has "the LORD", as Psalms 42–83 often do; it lacks "may it please you" (40:13) and "to sweep it away" (40:14); 70:3 has "turn back" where 40:15 has "be stunned" (one letter different in Hebrew); and 70:5 asks God to "hurry to me" where 40:17 says "may the Lord keep me in mind". See Psalm 70 for that psalm's own notes. Most scholars think the prayer existed separately and was attached to the thanksgiving of 40:1–12, or lifted from it.

a: be stunned because of their shame
t: As a result of their shame
p: 'Al-'eqev boshtam: "on account of their shame". 'Eqev is literally "heel", the consequence that follows.
b: 'Eqev ("heel") is used for what comes at the end, the result or reward (KJV "for a reward of their shame"). Psalm 70:3 has the same phrase with "turn back" (yashuvu) instead of "be stunned" (yashommu).

a: As for me, I am poor and needy
p: 'Ani ve'evyon, "poor and needy", is the self-name of those who have only God to rely on.
b: The pair 'ani ve'evyon occurs often in the psalms (35:10; 37:14; 70:5; 86:1; 109:22). It may describe real poverty, but in prayer it also names an attitude: helpless before enemies, the speaker throws himself on God. Even the king could pray this way.

a: Happy is the one who pays attention to the weak
p: Maskil el-dal: "one who gives thought to the weak". The Talmud reads dal as the sick and draws the duty to visit them.
b: Maskil (the word of the 32:0 title) here means to pay careful attention. Dal is someone weak, poor, or thin with sickness. The psalm is about a sick man (41:3, 8), so the rabbis read the verse of visiting the sick: "whoever visits the sick is saved from the judgment of Gehenna", citing this verse (Talmud, Nedarim 40a). The Greek adds "and needy"; see the variant. Psalm 41 opens with "Happy" (ashrei), as Psalm 1 does, so Book I begins and ends with the same word.

a: Do not hand him over to the greed of his enemies.
p: The line turns from talking about God to talking to him, a common shift in Hebrew prayer.
b: Verses 1–3 speak about the LORD in the third person, but this line addresses him directly, and so does 41:3b. Hebrew poetry moves easily between "he" and "you" for God. "Greed" is nefesh, here the appetite or desire of the enemies (as in 27:12). The verb before it, "he will be called happy", has two spellings in the manuscripts (the Ketiv and Qere), with no difference in meaning.

a: you make over his whole bed
p: Literally "all his bed you have turned in his illness": probably, God restores the sick man to health.
b: Kol-mishkavo hafakhta becholyo. Hafakh is to turn or overturn. Readings: (1) God turns the sickbed into a bed of health (most modern scholars); (2) he makes the bed for the sick man, like a nurse (KJV "thou wilt make all his bed"); (3) he overturns the sickness itself. The verse is a promise for those who care for the weak: God will care for them when they are weak.

a: heal my very self, because I have sinned against you
p: The sick man asks for healing and confesses sin in the same breath. The Gospels join the two in Jesus' healings.
b: Refa'ah nafshi, "heal my soul" or "heal me", since nefesh is the whole living person. As in Psalm 38, the sufferer sees his illness as tied to sin, though the psalm does not say every sickness is punishment. Compare the paralyzed man whom Jesus forgives and heals (Mark 2:5–12) and James 5:15–16.

a: If one comes to visit, he speaks empty words
p: Visiting the sick was a duty. This visitor comes to gather gossip and spread it in the street.
b: In a village, neighbors came to sit with the sick. This visitor says the right things ("empty words", shav') while his heart collects material, and then "goes outside and talks". Job's friends also came to comfort and ended by accusing (Job 2:11; 16:2).

a: Something vile has been poured into him
p: Devar beliyya'al, "a thing of worthlessness", here means a deadly sickness, or a curse cast on him.
b: Beliyya'al usually describes worthless or wicked people ("worthless men", Deuteronomy 13:13; Judges 19:22). Here it is a davar, a thing or word: either a fatal disease "poured into" (yatsuq, cast like metal) his body, or an evil spell spoken over him. The name Belial later became a name for Satan (2 Corinthians 6:15) and is common in the Dead Sea Scrolls.

a: has raised his heel high against me
p: Jesus applies this verse to Judas at the Last Supper (John 13:18), leaving out "the one I trusted".
b: In John 13:18 Jesus says: "I am not speaking about all of you; I know whom I chose. But the Scripture must be fulfilled: The one who eats my bread has lifted his heel against me" (a fresh rendering). John's Greek is not the Septuagint's, and he drops "the one I trusted", perhaps because Jesus knew what Judas would do. In the psalm the friend may be a royal counselor; readers who follow the titles think of Ahithophel, who joined Absalom against David (2 Samuel 15:12, 31). Raising the heel may mean kicking out like a mule, or showing the sole of the foot as an insult.

a: so that I can pay them back
p: The sick man asks to be raised up so he can pay his enemies back. Readers have found this hard.
b: Wa'ashallemah lahem: "so I may pay them back". If the speaker is a king, repaying may mean doing justice: rulers were to punish treachery (compare 1 Kings 2:5–9). Others hear simple revenge, an honest feeling the psalms do not hide. Christian readers set it beside Romans 12:17–21; Augustine reads the payment as good for evil, or as Christ rising to judge. See the curse psalms topic.

a: in my integrity
p: Tummi, "my integrity", is the wholeness Job holds on to. It does not deny the sin of 41:4.
b: Tummah/tom is wholeheartedness, a life not split in two (Job 2:3; 27:5; Psalm 26:1). The same man has confessed sin (41:4). Integrity here is loyalty to God, not sinlessness. "Before your face" may refer to standing in the temple, or serving the king as an official stands before his lord.

a: Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel
p: Verse 13 is not part of Psalm 41 but the closing blessing of the first of the five books of Psalms.
b: Each of the first four books of Psalms ends with a doxology, a short blessing of God: here, 72:18–19, 89:52 and 106:48. Psalm 150 closes Book V as a whole psalm of praise. The words match 106:48 and the blessing at the end of David's song in 1 Chronicles 16:36. The Greek has "So be it, so be it" (genoito genoito) for "Amen and Amen". Jewish tradition compared the five books of Psalms to the five books of Moses (Midrash Tehillim 1:2). See book.json for the Psalter's shape.
